title: The NRI's Guide to Himachal Pradesh — Mountain Retreats, Toy Trains, and the Dalai Lama's Home
excerpt: When summer hits and the plains become unbearable, every Indian family for generations has done the same thing — headed for the hills.
body:
## Why Himachal Pradesh?

When summer hits and the plains become unbearable, every Indian family for generations has done the same thing — headed for the hills. Himachal Pradesh is India's original escape. For NRIs visiting India in summer with parents and children in tow, Himachal offers cool mountain air, genuine Himalayan scenery, and a pace of life so different from American suburbia that it functions as therapy. Shimla's colonial architecture recalls a different era. Manali's adventure sports keep teenagers engaged. And Dharamshala — home to the Dalai Lama and Tibet's government-in-exile — offers a spiritual dimension that no other hill station in India can match.

## Top Experiences

**1. Rohtang Pass & Atal Tunnel** — The 10-km Atal Tunnel (opened 2020) connects Manali to Lahaul-Spiti, making what was once a dangerous seasonal road into a year-round route. Drive through the tunnel to Sissu on the other side for stark, beautiful Spiti Valley landscapes. Rohtang Pass itself (13,050 feet) is snow-covered even in June.

**2. Old Manali & Solang Valley** — Old Manali has evolved from a backpacker village into a vibrant café and culture scene. Solang Valley offers paragliding, zorbing, and skiing in winter. The Beas River runs through everything.

**3. McLeod Ganj & Tsuglagkhang Complex** — Visit the Dalai Lama's residence and the Tibetan museum. The Bhagsu Waterfall trail is an easy 45-minute walk. McLeod Ganj has some of the best Tibetan food in the world — momos, thukpa, and butter tea.

**4. Shimla Ridge & Mall Road** — The former summer capital of British India still carries that colonial charm. Walk the Ridge at sunset, visit Christ Church, and take the heritage toy train from Kalka to Shimla — a UNESCO World Heritage railway.

**5. Kasol & Kheerganga Trek** — The Parvati Valley draws both adventure seekers and those looking for solitude. Kasol is the base camp. The Kheerganga trek (12 km one way) ends at natural hot springs at 3,050 metres. Camp overnight for the stars.

## Getting There

Kullu-Manali Airport has flights from Delhi (1.5 hours) but the small runway means flights are weather-dependent and frequently cancelled. More reliable: fly into Chandigarh and drive to Shimla (4 hours) or Manali (8 hours). The Kalka-Shimla toy train is a scenic 5-hour journey. From the US, fly into Delhi, spend a night, then fly or drive to Himachal. For Dharamshala/McLeod Ganj, fly into Gaggal Airport (Kangra) from Delhi. Road trips from Delhi to Manali via Chandigarh take 10–12 hours — hire a driver, do not self-drive on mountain roads unless experienced.

## Where to Stay

Shimla: Oberoi Cecil and Wildflower Hall are the luxury picks. For heritage, try Hotel Woodville Palace. Budget options on Mall Road start at ₹1,500. Manali: Zostel and Moustache for backpackers, Johnson Lodge and Span Resorts for mid-range, The Himalayan for luxury. McLeod Ganj: Hyatt Regency Dharamshala is surprisingly accessible. Kasol: Riverside camps and guesthouses dominate — Parvati Kuteer and The Hosteller are popular. During peak season (May–June, October), book everything a month in advance.

## Food & the Desi Connection

Himachali cuisine is underrated. Siddu (steamed bread with walnut filling), dham (festival thali with rajma, chole, and rice), and Kullu trout are local specialties. Manali's Old Town is packed with cafés serving Israeli, Italian, and Tibetan food alongside Punjabi dhabas. McLeod Ganj momos — steamed or fried, stuffed with vegetables or chicken — are among the best you will eat anywhere. Shimla's Indian Coffee House on Mall Road has been serving filter coffee and samosas since the 1950s. For NRI families craving comfort food, North Indian cuisine is everywhere and excellent.

## NRI Tips

Indian passport holders and OCI cardholders need no special permits for most of Himachal. Inner Line Permits are required for Spiti Valley beyond Kaza and certain areas near the Tibetan border — apply online through the Himachal tourism portal. Currency is INR. UPI and card payments work in towns but fail in valleys — carry cash for Kasol, Kheerganga, and Spiti. Mobile coverage drops to zero in remote areas — download offline maps. Altitude sickness is real above 3,000 metres — acclimatise gradually if heading to Rohtang or Spiti. Roads are dangerous during monsoon (July–August) — landslides are common. The best months are March to June and September to November. Pack layers regardless of season — mountain weather changes in minutes.
